v.why: Large batches give few, low-noise steps in a fixed epoch budget, so a higher lr relieves undertraining without the noise that destabilizes small-batch runs.
Deeper stacks compound Adam's per-parameter updates, moving the divergence cliff to lower lr.
Wide layers sum many Adam updates so the function-space step grows with width and crosses the instability threshold earlier.
Averaging more samples tames the gradient noise that drives high-lr Adam into divergence.
Penalty is normalized per batch so small batches feel an effectively stronger L2, and raising alpha there tips into underfitting.
Depth supplies missing capacity for narrow nets that cannot get it from width.
High lr compounds across extra layers into exploding or dead ReLU activations.
Strong L2 shrinks every layer so the product of weights collapses multiplicatively with depth.
With a single hidden layer width is the only capacity route, so it pays off most there.
At low lr wider layers move further in function space per step and avoid undertraining.
